newsitem.title: PERU: Peru, MRTA restart peace talks after boycotts.
newsitem.headline: Peru, MRTA restart peace talks after boycotts.

text.p: The Peruvian government and Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima restarted talks on Wednesday aimed at ending the 85-day crisis peacefully.
A white Red Cross car drove the spokesmen for the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) across the street from the residence to a safe house where nine previous rounds of talks were held.
A rebel told Reuters by walkie-talkie radio from inside the besieged mansion that both the MRTA's leader, Nestor Cerpa, and his second-in-command, Rolly Rojas, were inside the car.
Waiting in the Red Cross safe house for the meeting was government negotiator Domingo Palermo.

As the Red Cross car pulled out of the compound, the 20-odd hostage-takers who remained at the residence sang their rebel hymn in honour of MRTA members killed in fighting with Peru's security forces.

The three guarantors overseeing negotiations -- Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, for the Vatican, Canadian ambassador Anthony Vincent, and Red Cross chief representative Michel Minnig -- attended the meeting, which was the 10th round of talks since Feb. 11. Japanese government observer, Terusuke Terada, was also present.
The first face-to-face dialogue in a week was possible after the guarantors commission held meetings over the last two days with Cerpa and Palermo to coax the two sides back to the negotiating table.
Until last week, the talks to end the siege peacefully seemed to be progressing steadily.
But last Thursday the rebels refused to attend talks charging the government with planning to take the building by storm through a secret tunnel.

After energetic meetings with both sides, the guarantors arranged for a fresh round of talks on Monday, only to have the government abruptly call off that meeting, accusing the rebels of trying to backtrack on the progress already made.
Before Wednesday's talks, President Alberto Fujimori continued his propaganda trail around traditionally strong rebel areas in the Amazon jungle to win the hearts and minds of peasants.

"Even in this part of the jungle, so far from the capital, people want peace. They do not want violence. They do not want these movements calling themselves revolutionaries," Fujimori told the villagers of Papaplaya in the Huallaga valley 600 miles (960 km) to the north of Lima.

On the second day of a tour to the northern jungle, the president followed his inauguration of government-financed works on Tuesday by handing out clothes and blankets to peasants left homeless from recent flash-floods around the region.

The United Nations Human Rights Commission also had harsh words for the MRTA on Wednesday. In a statement issued from Geneva, the commission condemned the rebels as "terrorist elements" and said hostage-taking anywhere violated human rights.

The siege began Dec. 17 when the rebels blasted into a cocktail party hosted by the Japanese ambassador and took all the guests hostage. The rebels released most of them in the first few days, but kept some as bargaining chips, including Fujimori's brother Pedro, two of his cabinet ministers, the Japanese ambassador and a long list of Japanese businessmen.

The 72 men held by the MRTA, who are demanding freedom for about 400 jailed comrades, are basically in good health but are showing growing signs of chronic stress, including gum disease and skin ailments, after 85 days in captivity, said a doctor who is accompanying a Red Cross team treating them.
